tldr: Rotsaert shows how ArchUnit turns architecture rules into JUnit tests and how the Taikai library on top of it provides ready-made, readable rules for Java and Spring projects.
summary: Rotsaert starts from familiar drift in a layered Spring Boot app: a repository injected into a controller, a domain class depending on a service, cycles too long to spot in review, and a utils class half the code depends on. Code review fails on large, often AI-generated PRs, so he tests the architecture instead. ArchUnit expresses rules as JUnit tests (@AnalyzeClasses, @ArchTest) and has a pre-built layeredArchitecture() rule. But starting from a blank test is hard, the documentation is long, and the rules grow repetitive. Taikai sits on ArchUnit and offers a builder with predefined rules by category: Java, logging, test, and Spring controllers, services and repositories.

His demos ban Lombok imports, forbid methods that declare generic exceptions (with a documented exclusion for one Spring Security config class), and chain existing rules into a house convention for Spring configuration: config classes in a config package, immutable records with @ConfigurationProperties, and @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the main class. Generated code is excluded, checkAll() reports every violation, and a company default config can be extended per project. When no Taikai rule exists, a plain ArchUnit rule plugs into the builder. His team had AI generate ArchUnit rules from their SonarQube instance through the SonarQube MCP server, so AI-written code fails the gate less often.
keyPoints: ArchUnit rules run as JUnit tests on every build; use ImportOption to keep them from applying to test classes.
Taikai pulls in ArchUnit transitively and replaces class-level annotations with a builder (namespace, categories, build, check or checkAll).
Any Taikai rule can exclude specific classes or regex patterns, which documents deliberate exceptions in the test itself.
Generating ArchUnit rules from existing SonarQube rules with an AI model and the SonarQube MCP server reduced quality-gate failures on AI-generated code.

Adoption only happened once the Taikai test was added to the team's Maven archetype for new projects; Rotsaert judges the single-maintainer library acceptable because it is quick to release and easy to fork.
takeaways: Copy the ready-made Taikai test (or the Spring Boot starter example) from its documentation into a project and run it.
Add rules one at a time when you see a recurring problem, and only enforce what matters, more strictly where AI writes the code.
Put architecture tests in your project archetype or template so new projects get them by default.

quotes.text: This is what I call configuration roulette. You search for all the annotations which contain the word configuration and then you add them.

watchIf: Your architecture diagrams no longer match the code and you want a quick, low-effort way to enforce layering and conventions in CI.
